title: Samantha Ruth Prabhu Touches Her In-Laws' Feet in the First Scene. Then She Picks Up a Gun. She Also Produced the Film.
excerpt: Maa Inti Bangaram, releasing June 19, is the first Telugu action film that Samantha has both starred in and bankrolled. It's a bet that the market for women with weapons exists — just not in Hindi.
body:
The trailer for *Maa Inti Bangaram* opens with Samantha Ruth Prabhu in a silk saree, touching the feet of her in-laws, folding her hands, smiling at the camera with the practiced demeanor of a new daughter-in-law who knows exactly what is expected of her.

Then she picks up a gun.

Samantha's new film — releasing June 19 — is a Telugu action comedy directed by Nandini Reddy that takes the "perfect bahu" trope of Indian family cinema and flips it into a survival thriller. She plays a woman with a hidden past who marries into a traditional family, only to have that past catch up with her in spectacularly violent fashion.

It is also, quietly, the most significant strategic move of her career.

## Producer, Star, Brand

*Maa Inti Bangaram* is not just a vehicle for Samantha. She is producing it. Her banner, Tralala Moving Pictures, is co-producing alongside Raj Nidimoru's D2R Films. This is the first Telugu film where Samantha has had creative and financial control from inception.

The distinction matters. After her divorce from Naga Chaitanya in 2021 and her public battle with myositis — a rare autoimmune condition that forced her to step away from acting for nearly a year — Samantha returned to the industry with a clarity of purpose that her earlier career lacked. She is no longer waiting for roles. She is creating them.

## The Action Pivot

The trailer has Samantha performing hand-to-hand combat sequences, wielding firearms, and engaging in the kind of choreographed violence that Bollywood typically reserves for its male stars. She does most of it in traditional Indian attire — a deliberate choice that the film's marketing has leaned into heavily.

Gulshan Devaiah plays the antagonist, a character described as "chaotic yet composed." Nandini Reddy, known for lighthearted Telugu romances like *Ala Modalaindi*, is working outside her comfort zone with action set pieces that the trailer suggests are substantial, not decorative.

The film was originally scheduled for May 15 but was pushed to June 19 to avoid the *Peddi* juggernaut — Ram Charan's sports drama opens June 4 and is expected to dominate Telugu screens for at least two weeks.

## Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

Samantha has one of the most engaged diaspora fanbases in South Indian cinema. Her split from Naga Chaitanya played out partly on American and European entertainment news sites. Her myositis announcement was covered by health publications outside India. Her *Oo Antava* dance number from *Pushpa* became a wedding staple from Houston to Harrow.

*Maa Inti Bangaram* — which translates roughly to "Our Family's Gold" — is positioned as the kind of film that NRI audiences will recognize: a woman navigating the expectations of a traditional Indian family while hiding something enormous about herself. The metaphor is not subtle, and it doesn't need to be.

## The June Battlefield

June 2026 is shaping up to be the most crowded month for Indian cinema this year. Ram Charan's *Peddi* (June 4), Madhuri Dixit's Netflix debut *Maa Behen* (June 4), Imtiaz Ali's partition drama *Main Vaapas Aaunga* with Diljit Dosanjh (June 12), and now Samantha's *Maa Inti Bangaram* (June 19) are all competing for audience attention in the same 30-day window.

For Samantha, the timing is deliberate. By releasing two weeks after *Peddi*, she avoids a head-to-head collision with the biggest Telugu film of the summer while still capitalizing on the foot traffic that Ram Charan's film will have generated in theatres.

## What's at Stake

This is a test case for a model that barely exists in Indian cinema: a female star producing and headlining her own action film. Kangana Ranaut has done versions of this (*Dhaakad*, *Tejas*), but the box office results were catastrophic. Samantha, by choosing Telugu over Hindi and action-comedy over grim action drama, is making a bet that the audience for female-led action is larger than Bollywood's recent results suggest — it's just not in Hindi.

If *Maa Inti Bangaram* works, it validates a path that other South Indian actresses — Nayanthara, Keerthy Suresh, Rashmika Mandanna — could follow. If it doesn't, it becomes another data point in the argument that Indian audiences won't buy tickets for women holding guns.

Samantha is betting they will. She put her own money on it.
